claim: The study analyzed data from 357 hospital wards in the region of Lyon, France.
source: We analyzed pathogen isolation incidence in clinical samples, antibiotic use, and patient transfers in 357 hospital wards from the region of Lyon, France.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the study setting.

claim: Data were collected from October 2016 to September 2017.
source: Data for all three measures were collected during the same period from October 2016 to September 2017.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the study period.

claim: The hospital network contained a total of 4,685 beds.
source: The hospital network contained a total of 4,685 beds.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the hospital network.

claim: The median ward size was 12 beds with an interquartile range of 5 to 20.
source: The median ward size was 12 beds (interquartile range, 5 to 20).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing ward characteristics.

claim: Ward-level data were aggregated from 13,915 infection episodes.
source: Ward-level data were aggregated from 13,915 infection episodes, defined as ward admissions with ≥1 clinical sample positive for E. coli or one of the so-called ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter cloacae complex), collectively termed ESKAPE2 (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the data collection.

claim: The median yearly incidence of infection episodes per ward was 24 with an interquartile range of 7 to 55.
source: The median yearly incidence of infection episodes per ward was 24 (interquartile range, 7 to 55).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing infection incidence.

claim: E. coli infections accounted for 6,303 episodes (45.3% of total).
source: E. coli	Susceptible to 3GC and carbapenems	EC	6,303 (45.3)	328 (91.9)	0.6 (0.6, 0.7)
evidence: Directly stated in Table 1 showing distribution of pathogen infection episodes.

claim: 3GC-resistant E. coli infections accounted for 737 episodes (5.3% of total).
evidence: Directly stated in Table 1 showing distribution of pathogen infection episodes.

claim: Carbapenem-resistant E. coli infections accounted for 24 episodes (0.2% of total).
source: Carbapenem-resistant	CREC	24 (0.2)	24 (5.6)	1.4 (0.0, 3.9)
evidence: Directly stated in Table 1 showing distribution of pathogen infection episodes.

claim: Vancomycin-resistant E. faecium infections were exceptional with only seven episodes.
source: Infections with vancomycin-resistant E. faecium and carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii were exceptional, with seven and twelve episodes respectively (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing rare infection types.

claim: Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii infections were exceptional with only twelve episodes.
source: Infections with vancomycin-resistant E. faecium and carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii were exceptional, with seven and twelve episodes respectively (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing rare infection types.

claim: Resistant variants were consistently less frequent than their less-resistant counterparts in all species.
source: Resistant variants were consistently less frequent than their less-resistant counterparts in all species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In enterobacteria, carbapenem-resistant variants were consistently less frequent than 3GC-resistant variants.
source: In enterobacteria (E. coli, K. pneumoniae and E. cloacae), carbapenem-resistant variants were consistently less frequent than 3GC-resistant variants.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing resistance patterns.

claim: The concentration of infection episodes was weak (<5%) for all variants.
source: The concentration of infection episodes was weak (<5%) for all variants, indicating a global lack of clustering (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by Table 1 data.

claim: Concentration increased with resistance (~2-fold increase from the least to the most resistant variant) in E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii.
source: Concentration increased with resistance (~2-fold increase from the least to the most resistant variant) in E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii, suggesting an adaptation of resistant variants to more specific wards within the hospital network compared to their less-resistant, less-concentrated counterparts.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing concentration patterns.

claim: Increased concentration with resistance suggests an adaptation of resistant variants to more specific wards within the hospital network.
source: Concentration increased with resistance (~2-fold increase from the least to the most resistant variant) in E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii, suggesting an adaptation of resistant variants to more specific wards within the hospital network compared to their less-resistant, less-concentrated counterparts.
evidence: Directly stated as an interpretation of the concentration data.

claim: The concentration pattern was not found in E. cloacae complex, E. faecium or S. aureus.
source: This pattern was not found in E. cloacae complex, E. faecium or S. aureus, in which the concentration index remained comparable across resistance categories.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing concentration patterns.

claim: Antibiotics were prescribed in 86.3% of wards.
source: Over the same period (October 2016 to September 2017), antibiotics were prescribed in 86.3% of wards (Table 2), with a total consumption of 125.7 defined daily doses per year per bed (ddd/y/b).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic use.

claim: Total antibiotic consumption was 125.7 defined daily doses per year per bed.
source: Over the same period (October 2016 to September 2017), antibiotics were prescribed in 86.3% of wards (Table 2), with a total consumption of 125.7 defined daily doses per year per bed (ddd/y/b).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic use.

claim: Antibiotic use was diffuse with concentration indices < 4%.
source: Antibiotic use was diffuse, with concentration indices < 4%, ranging from 0.8% for cefotaxime-ceftriaxone and fluoroquinolones to 3.6% for oxacillin.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic distribution.

claim: Ward-level antibiotic consumption volume had a stronger influence on the incidence of the more resistant pathogens.
source: We found that ward-level antibiotic consumption volume had a stronger influence on the incidence of the more resistant pathogens, while connectivity had the most influence on hospital-endemic species and carbapenem-resistant pathogens.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Connectivity had the most influence on hospital-endemic species and carbapenem-resistant pathogens.
source: We found that ward-level antibiotic consumption volume had a stronger influence on the incidence of the more resistant pathogens, while connectivity had the most influence on hospital-endemic species and carbapenem-resistant pathogens.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Piperacillin-tazobactam consumption was the strongest predictor of the cumulative incidence of infections resistant to empirical sepsis therapy.
source: Piperacillin-tazobactam consumption was the strongest predictor of the cumulative incidence of infections resistant to empirical sepsis therapy.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Global antibiotic use was associated with infection incidence in seven pathogen variants independent of connectivity, ward size, and ward type.
source: In these GLMs, global antibiotic use was associated with infection incidence in seven pathogen variants independent of connectivity, ward size, and ward type (Figure 1), including five resistant variants (3GC-resistant E. coli, 3GC-resistant K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, 3GC-resistant E. cloacae, and carbapenem-resistant E. cloacae) and two less-resistant variants (P. aeruginosa and E. faecium).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: Every doubling of antibiotic use predicted a 47% increase in carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae incidence (95% CI, 19% to 90%).
source: The largest effect size was found in carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, in which every doubling of antibiotic use predicted a 47% increase in incidence (95% confidence interval, 19% to 90%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: Connectivity predicted a higher incidence in all variants of P. aeruginosa and E. faecium.
source: Connectivity predicted a higher incidence in all variants of P. aeruginosa and E. faecium, with a stronger effect size in the resistant variants (11.5 and 43.7%, respectively) compared to their less-resistant counterparts (6.1 and 15.3%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: Connectivity had a stronger effect size in resistant variants of P. aeruginosa (11.5%) compared to less-resistant counterparts (6.1%).
source: Connectivity predicted a higher incidence in all variants of P. aeruginosa and E. faecium, with a stronger effect size in the resistant variants (11.5 and 43.7%, respectively) compared to their less-resistant counterparts (6.1 and 15.3%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: Connectivity had a stronger effect size in resistant variants of E. faecium (43.7%) compared to less-resistant counterparts (15.3%).
source: Connectivity predicted a higher incidence in all variants of P. aeruginosa and E. faecium, with a stronger effect size in the resistant variants (11.5 and 43.7%, respectively) compared to their less-resistant counterparts (6.1 and 15.3%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: A significant association with connectivity was found for less-resistant E. coli with a small effect size (2.6%).
source: A significant association with connectivity was also found for the less-resistant E. coli, although with a much smaller effect size (2.6%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: Ward size did not predict incidence in any variant.
source: Ward size did not predict incidence in any variant.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing GLM results.

claim: The mean percent change in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume in possibly selective associations was 6.5%.
source: The mean percent change in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume in possibly selective associations was 6.5%, compared to 0.9% in other associations (95% CI of the difference of the means, 0.6 to 10.6%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing possibly selective associations.

claim: The mean percent change in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume in other associations was 0.9%.
source: The mean percent change in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume in possibly selective associations was 6.5%, compared to 0.9% in other associations (95% CI of the difference of the means, 0.6 to 10.6%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing possibly selective associations.

claim: Three of the four strongest possibly selective associations involved cefotaxime-ceftriaxone.
source: Three of the four strongest possibly selective associations involved cefotaxime-ceftriaxone, which selected for 3GC-resistant E. coli, K. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa; the other involved carbapenems selecting for carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing possibly selective associations.

claim: Antibiotic use was the strongest predictor of the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections (6.5% increase per doubling, 95% CI, 2.5 to 11.0%).
source: In these models, antibiotic use was the strongest predictor of the incidence of both carbapenem-resistant (6.5% increase in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume, 95% CI, 2.5 to 11.0%) and 3GC-resistant infections (5.1% increase, 95% CI, 2.7 to 7.5%; Figure 3a).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing cumulative resistance models.

claim: Antibiotic use was the strongest predictor of the incidence of 3GC-resistant infections (5.1% increase per doubling, 95% CI, 2.7 to 7.5%).
source: In these models, antibiotic use was the strongest predictor of the incidence of both carbapenem-resistant (6.5% increase in incidence for every doubling of consumption volume, 95% CI, 2.5 to 11.0%) and 3GC-resistant infections (5.1% increase, 95% CI, 2.7 to 7.5%; Figure 3a).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing cumulative resistance models.

claim: Connectivity better predicted the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections (4.8%, 95% CI, −0.4 to 10.7%) compared with 3GC-resistant infections (1.0%, 95% CI, −2.3 to 4.5%).
source: Connectivity better predicted the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections (4.8%, 95% CI, −0.4 to 10.7%) compared with 3GC-resistant infections (1.0%, 95% CI, −2.3 to 4.5%), in line with the comparatively stronger association of connectivity with the incidence of individual carbapenem-resistant variants (Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing cumulative resistance models.

claim: The use of piperacillin-tazobactam predicted the incidence of 3GC-resistant infections (5.9% increase, 95% CI, 2.9 to 9.0%).
source: Strikingly, the use of piperacillin-tazobactam predicted the incidence of both 3GC-resistant (5.9% increase, 95% CI, 2.9 to 9.0%) and carbapenem-resistant infections (10.3% increase, 95% CI, 5.0 to 16.0%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic-specific associations.

claim: The use of piperacillin-tazobactam predicted the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections (10.3% increase, 95% CI, 5.0 to 16.0%).
source: Strikingly, the use of piperacillin-tazobactam predicted the incidence of both 3GC-resistant (5.9% increase, 95% CI, 2.9 to 9.0%) and carbapenem-resistant infections (10.3% increase, 95% CI, 5.0 to 16.0%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic-specific associations.

claim: The incidence of 3GC-resistant infections was predicted by the consumption of cefotaxime-ceftriaxone (4.8% increase, 95% CI, 1.5 to 8.2%) but not carbapenems (1.4% increase, 95% CI, −1.7 to 4.6%).
source: The incidence of 3GC-resistant infections was predicted by the consumption of cefotaxime-ceftriaxone (4.8% increase, 95% CI, 1.5 to 8.2%) but not carbapenems (1.4% increase, 95% CI, −1.7 to 4.6%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic-specific associations.

claim: The use of carbapenems predicted the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections with a wide uncertainty margin (5.1% increase, 95% CI, −0.6 to 11.1%).
source: In the same vein, the use of carbapenems, but not 3GCs, predicted the incidence of carbapenem-resistant infections, although with a wide uncertainty margin (5.1% increase, 95% CI, −0.6 to 11.1%).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing antibiotic-specific associations.

claim: Hospitals continue to be important hotspots for AMR in clinically-relevant pathogens due to the confluence of strong antibiotic selection pressure, fragile patients, and highly resistant pathogens that can disseminate between wards and facilities through patient transfers.
source: However, hospitals continue to be important hotspots for AMR in clinically-relevant pathogens (Chatterjee et al., 2018; David et al., 2019) due to the confluence of strong antibiotic selection pressure, fragile patients, and highly resistant pathogens that can disseminate between wards and facilities through patient transfers (Safdar and Maki, 2002; Snitkin et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hospitals become reservoirs of resistant bacteria.
source: These conditions result in hospitals becoming reservoirs of resistant bacteria (Clarivet et al., 2016; Cohen, 1992; Pogue et al., 2013), which can later enter the community (Huttner et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Resistant bacteria from hospitals can later enter the community.
source: These conditions result in hospitals becoming reservoirs of resistant bacteria (Clarivet et al., 2016; Cohen, 1992; Pogue et al., 2013), which can later enter the community (Huttner et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The primary hospital-based strategies against AMR are antimicrobial stewardship and infection control.
source: The primary hospital-based strategies against AMR are antimicrobial stewardship, which aims to lower the antibiotic pressure, and infection control whose goal is to reduce the transmission of pathogens (Manning et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: The association between antibiotic use and resistance is not uniform across pathogen species.
source: This is further complicated by the fact that the association between antibiotic use and resistance is not uniform across pathogen species (Bell et al., 2014) or classes of antibiotics (Niehus et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The association between antibiotic use and resistance is not uniform across classes of antibiotics.
source: This is further complicated by the fact that the association between antibiotic use and resistance is not uniform across pathogen species (Bell et al., 2014) or classes of antibiotics (Niehus et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metapopulation ecology was introduced by Levins in 1969 to explain the persistence of agricultural pests across a set of habitat patches.
source: Metapopulation ecology is such a framework. It was introduced by Levins, 1969 to explain the persistence of agricultural pests across a set of habitat patches, such as crop fields, and refined by Hanski to account for the characteristics of patches, such as their size, and the connectivity between them (Hanski, 1998; Hanski, 1994).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metapopulation models of hospital AMR have been applied to simulated rather than empirical data.
source: So far, however, metapopulation models of hospital AMR have been applied to simulated rather than empirical data (Spagnolo et al., 2018; Vilches et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The influence of connectivity on the incidence of a pathogen variant is expected to be higher if the variant is endemic to the hospital.
source: In our closed network model of the hospital, the influence of connectivity on the incidence of a pathogen variant is expected to be higher if the variant is endemic to the hospital, its prevalence varies across wards, and changes from one variant category to another are rare.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion as a theoretical interpretation.

claim: The influence of connectivity is strongest in the hospital-endemic pathogens P. aeruginosa and E. faecium.
source: Consistent with this theoretical interpretation of connectivity, we found that its influence was strongest in the hospital-endemic pathogens P. aeruginosa and E. faecium (Blanc et al., 2007; Wurster et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: MRSA incidence was not predicted by connectivity.
source: Intriguingly, MRSA incidence was not predicted by connectivity.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion.

claim: In France, the proportions of MRSA among S. aureus are comparable in community and hospital settings, at about 10%.
source: In France, the proportions of MRSA among S. aureus are comparable in community and hospital settings, at about 10% (ECDC, 2019; ONERBA France, 2018; Santé Publique France, 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: MRSA population structures in hospitals and the community are comparably dominated by the so-called ST8 Lyon clone.
source: MRSA population structures in hospitals and the community are comparably dominated by the so-called ST8 Lyon clone which is equally found in in- and outpatients (Dauwalder et al., 2008).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: Connectivity was a comparatively weaker predictor for community-associated variants (3GC-resistant E. coli and K. pneumoniae) that enter from outside the hospital network.
source: Contrasting with hospital-endemic pathogens, connectivity was a comparatively weaker predictor for community-associated variants (3GC-resistant E. coli and K. pneumoniae) that enter from outside the hospital network, and in variants whose resistance is selected locally because they can frequently shift between susceptible and resistant categories.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The weak association of connectivity with the incidence of resistant E. cloacae complex variants might be explained by the plasticity of their resistance profile.
source: Indeed, the weak association of connectivity with the incidence of resistant E. cloacae complex variants, for instance, might be explained by the plasticity of their resistance profile, facilitating their local selection.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: E. cloacae complex can resist cephalosporins and carbapenems through increased AmpC beta-lactamase and decreased porin expression.
source: While resistance in E. coli and K. pneumoniae typically requires gene acquisition (Manges et al., 2019; Wyres and Holt, 2016), E. cloacae complex can resist cephalosporins and carbapenems through increased AmpC beta-lactamase and decreased porin expression (Pavez et al., 2016; Babouee Flury et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Resistance in E. coli and K. pneumoniae typically requires gene acquisition.
source: While resistance in E. coli and K. pneumoniae typically requires gene acquisition (Manges et al., 2019; Wyres and Holt, 2016), E. cloacae complex can resist cephalosporins and carbapenems through increased AmpC beta-lactamase and decreased porin expression (Pavez et al., 2016; Babouee Flury et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Piperacillin-tazobactam has been repeatedly considered as an alternative drug of choice in carbapenem-sparing strategies based on its in vitro efficacy against ESBL-producing enterobacteria.
source: Based on its in vitro efficacy against extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing enterobacteria, piperacillin-tazobactam has been repeatedly considered as an alternative drug of choice in carbapenem-sparing strategies (Harris et al., 2015; Peterson, 2008).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In several recent reports including a multicenter randomized clinical trial, piperacillin-tazobactam treatment of sepsis with ESBL-producing enterobacteria was associated with poorer outcomes compared to carbapenem treatment.
source: Yet, in several recent reports including a multicenter randomized clinical trial, piperacillin-tazobactam treatment of sepsis with ESBL-producing enterobacteria was associated with poorer outcomes compared to carbapenem treatment (Harris et al., 2018; Ofer-Friedman et al., 2015; Tamma et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: At the population level, the incidence of carbapenem-resistant enterobacteria was negatively associated with the use of piperacillin-tazobactam in a 5 year, single-hospital trend analysis study.
source: At the population level, the incidence of carbapenem-resistant enterobacteria was negatively associated with the use of piperacillin-tazobactam in a 5 year, single-hospital trend analysis study (McLaughlin et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: At the patient level, the exposure to piperacillin-tazobactam was associated with the acquisition of carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in a meta-analysis.
source: At the patient level, however, the exposure to piperacillin-tazobactam was associated with the acquisition of carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in a meta-analysis (Raman et al., 2018) and carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli in a single-hospital prospective cohort study (Marchenay et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The exposure to piperacillin-tazobactam was associated with the acquisition of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli in a single-hospital prospective cohort study.
source: At the patient level, however, the exposure to piperacillin-tazobactam was associated with the acquisition of carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in a meta-analysis (Raman et al., 2018) and carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli in a single-hospital prospective cohort study (Marchenay et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The study did not consider the role of healthcare workers in pathogen transmission.
source: First, we did not consider the role of healthcare workers in pathogen transmission, nor the role of direct patient admissions from the community.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion as a study limitation.

claim: The study did not consider the role of direct patient admissions from the community.
source: First, we did not consider the role of healthcare workers in pathogen transmission, nor the role of direct patient admissions from the community.

source: Third, the small sample sizes of resistant variants of E. faecium and A. baumannii limited our ability to draw robust inferences regarding these variants and further studies are required to confirm these results (Arias and Murray, 2012; Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: The findings reflect the AMR ecology of a Western European area with generally lower prevalences of carbapenemase-producing pathogens, vancomycin-resistant E. faecium, and MRSA than in other regions of the world.
source: Finally, our findings reflect the AMR ecology of a Western European area, with generally lower prevalences of carbapenemase-producing pathogens, vancomycin-resistant E. faecium, and MRSA than in other regions of the world.

claim: Both antibiotic use and inter-ward connectivity may predict the burden of AMR in a variant-specific fashion.
source: To conclude, the modeling of the incidence of infections with seven major bacterial species and their drug-resistant variants in hospital wards using a metapopulation framework indicates that both antibiotic use and inter-ward connectivity may predict the burden of AMR in a variant-specific fashion.
evidence: Directly stated in the conclusion.

claim: Reducing connectivity with infection control interventions could be more effective at preventing the spread of carbapenem-resistant pathogens between wards compared to 3GC-resistant pathogens.
source: This suggests that reducing connectivity with infection control interventions could be more effective at preventing the spread of carbapenem-resistant pathogens between wards compared to 3GC-resistant pathogens.

source: Overall, the larger magnitude of the coefficients of possibly selective associations suggests that the local, ward-level selection of drug-resistant variants by antibiotics is measurably pervasive throughout our hospital network.

source: Bivariate analyses confirmed that the incidence control correlated with the observed cumulative incidence of all bacteria (R²=0.96, 95% CI, 0.95 to 0.96, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and, to a lesser extent, with the total antibiotic use (R²=0.34, 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.40, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: The incidence control correlated with total antibiotic use (R²=0.34, 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.40).
